title: From Missed Exam Cutoffs to Billionaire: How Aravind Srinivas Built Perplexity AI on Rejection
excerpt: The Chennai-born IIT Madras graduate turned early failures into fuel, building an AI search company now valued at over $22 billion and challenging Google's dominance.
body:
• Aravind Srinivas, 31, missed the computer science cutoff on India's JEE entrance exam twice — the electrical engineering path he took instead gave him a deeper technical foundation for AI research.
  • Perplexity AI, co-founded in 2022, has raised $1.72 billion across 11 funding rounds and reached a $22.6 billion valuation by January 2026, with 1,389 employees.
  • Srinivas became India's youngest billionaire in 2025 with an estimated net worth of ₹21,190 crore ($2.5 billion), after growing up in a lower-middle-class Chennai family.
  • A software engineer who turned down Srinivas's founding offer to stay at FTX later called it the "worst financial decision" of his life.

When Aravind Srinivas sat for India's Joint Entrance Examination, the gateway to the country's elite engineering colleges, he fell short of the computer science cutoff. He ended up at IIT Madras studying electrical engineering. When an opportunity arose to switch departments, he narrowly missed again.

Those twin rejections set the trajectory for what would become one of the most consequential careers in artificial intelligence.

An Unlikely Foundation

Growing up in a lower-middle-class family in Chennai, Srinivas has described the bar for success as simply landing a stable job. Getting into Google was the family's aspiration.

"All we wanted to do was get a job in Google. Being an engineer at Google was considered a win. I'm already doing remarkably well compared to that ambition we had as a family, so there's really nothing for me to lose."

— Aravind Srinivas, CEO, Perplexity AI

Rather than dwell on the CS department he couldn't enter, Srinivas realized electrical engineering gave him something arguably more valuable: a deep understanding of systems, signals, circuits, and the fundamentals of how computers actually work. That depth proved critical when he pivoted to AI research.

He taught himself Python, competed in Kaggle machine learning competitions, and landed a research internship with deep learning pioneer Yoshua Bengio. From there, he earned a spot in UC Berkeley's PhD program, followed by stints at OpenAI and Google DeepMind — the very company his family had dreamed he'd work for.

Building Where Others Weren't Looking

At Berkeley, Srinivas co-created a course on deep unsupervised learning in 2020, before "generative AI" entered the mainstream vocabulary. He kept turning to lab mate Peter Chen with a recurring question: "Hey, do you want to start a company with me?"

The idea that would become Perplexity started with an observation most dismissed as irrelevant: Google had dominated search for two decades, but it still returned lists of blue links. What if accessing information felt like talking to a research assistant?

In August 2022, Srinivas co-founded Perplexity AI with Denis Yarats, Johnny Ho, and Andy Konwinski. The company launched its AI-powered answer engine on December 7 that year.

The FTX Connection

Before Perplexity launched, Srinivas had reached out to Aditya Baradwaj, a software engineer, offering him a founding role. Baradwaj declined, choosing to stay at Alameda Research, the trading firm tied to Sam Bankman-Fried's FTX empire.

Months later, FTX collapsed in one of the largest financial frauds in history. Baradwaj went public with his regret in a post on X, sharing the original chat with Srinivas and writing, "I've got you beat for the worst financial decision."

Scale and Ambition

Perplexity's growth has been sharp. The company processed 780 million queries in May 2025, with more than 20% month-over-month growth and roughly 30 million queries daily. Revenue jumped from an annualized $35 million in August 2023 to $150 million by mid-2025. By January 2026, the company was valued at $22.6 billion, having raised $1.72 billion across 11 funding rounds from investors including Jeff Bezos, Nvidia, SoftBank, and Cristiano Ronaldo.

The ambitions have expanded accordingly. In January 2025, Perplexity submitted a merger proposal with TikTok US. That August, it made an unsolicited $34.5 billion bid for Google's Chrome browser, arguing the sale could resolve antitrust litigation against Alphabet. The company also launched Comet, an AI-powered browser for premium users.

Diaspora Resonance

In 2025, Srinivas debuted on the M3M Hurun India Rich List with an estimated net worth of ₹21,190 crore, making him India's youngest billionaire at 31. His story — from a Chennai classroom to the helm of a company challenging Google — has become a touchstone for the Indian diaspora and aspiring entrepreneurs across South Asia.

"I have nothing to lose. I came from nothing. I never even imagined myself to be doing all this. So my life has already been extraordinary beyond any level of imagination."

— Aravind Srinivas, on the 20CV with Harry Stebbings podcast

His philosophy on risk is blunt. In every setback — from missed exam cutoffs to the FTX engineer who bet against him — Srinivas has found confirmation of an approach he summarizes as: "Be on the offense all the time. Attack, attack, attack."

For the Indian-American tech community, his trajectory offers a counter-narrative to the well-worn paths through FAANG companies and venture capital. Sometimes, Srinivas suggests, the rejection letter is the real offer.
nri_angle: Chennai-born IIT Madras graduate Aravind Srinivas became India's youngest billionaire by turning early academic rejections into the foundation for Perplexity AI, now valued at $22.6 billion.
author: Diaspora Desk
